speaker: Petter Hörnfeldt
title: Ep16 - Interview with Petter Hoernfeldt - Mentour Pilot
question: In commercial aviation, what practical realities should aspiring pilots map out before committing to a flight-training route?
guest: When you get bitten by the bug, you have to start by sitting down and making a plan, checking what your potential paths are to achieving this goal. First is information gathering: are there any sponsored programs you can get into? In my case, there was a government-sponsored program with no airline affiliation that gave the training away to 30 people per year. I learned about it at 14, which gave me three years to improve my grades to guarantee an interview. If your country doesn't have a sponsored program, maybe an airline offers something similar. Another path is self-funded training, either done modularly or as a direct ab initio course—an intensive 18-month to two-year program. They differ in price and time, and both have pros and cons. It's really important at that stage to gather all information without bias, because some airlines only take cadets from schools they have approved, which you need to know if you're aiming for a specific airline. In some cases, you can cut your training cost in half by going modular, especially if you work at the same time to fund it. You need to know all of this before making any decisions.

points.note: Accept: target carriers may restrict entry-level hiring to partner or airline-approved academies, so school choice can gate eligibility. Do not credit: generic advice to pick a reputable or accredited school.

points.note: Accept: pacing modular ratings while holding a job allows pay-as-you-go financing instead of taking out massive upfront loans. Do not credit: generic budgeting advice not tied to modular training structure.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Before committing, get a first-class medical certificate: a disqualifying condition discovered after you've spent money is the most avoidable failure in this career. Everything else follows from that.

Next, map the full cost and timeline, not just the headline price. In the US, reaching airline minimums typically means 1,500 flight hours (less with certain degree or military pathways), often costing $80,000–$120,000 or more, followed by a year or two of low-paid hour-building, usually as a flight instructor. In Europe, integrated courses often exceed €100,000, and you graduate with around 200 hours but no guaranteed job.

Compare the route structures: integrated versus modular, university programmes, airline cadet schemes, or the military. Each trades cost, speed, flexibility and job linkage differently.

Scrutinise schools too. Check aircraft and instructor availability, real completion times and graduate placement, and avoid paying large sums upfront, since schools do go bust.

Finally, plan for the industry's cyclicality. Hiring swings sharply with the economy, seniority governs pay, bases and schedules, and early years often mean relocation and irregular rosters. Have a financing plan and a fallback that survive a downturn.

models.answer:
Before paying for flight lessons, aspiring commercial pilots should first secure a Class 1 medical certificate to confirm that no health, vision, or medication history will disqualify them later. Next, they must budget for realistic total costs rather than advertised minimums. Most students exceed statutory flight-hour requirements, and checkride fees, living expenses, weather delays, and high-interest loans add up quickly. Candidates should weigh flexible modular training against accelerated academies, university pathways, or airline cadet programs—while avoiding large upfront deposits that risk loss if a school closes, and checking aircraft availability and instructor-to-student ratios locally.

Equally critical is mapping the bridge between earning a commercial license around 250 hours and meeting airline hiring minimums, such as the 1,500-hour ATP threshold in the United States or multi-crew requirements elsewhere, which usually demands one to three years in modest-paying time-building jobs like flight instructing. Finally, pilots must prepare for cyclical airline hiring and a seniority-governed lifestyle marked by crew-base relocations, irregular schedules, reserve duty, and career-long medical and simulator evaluations.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5

Before choosing a route, aspiring pilots should first secure a first-class medical certificate, because a disqualifying condition makes every other investment pointless. Next comes the full cost. Getting from zero time to a commercial license with multi-engine and instrument ratings usually costs $80,000–$120,000 or more. On top of that come living expenses and possible type-rating fees, so you need to plan the financing, loan terms and repayment.

The choice of route also matters. An integrated academy or university program is faster and more structured, sometimes with airline pathway agreements. Modular or Part 61 training is cheaper and more flexible but needs self-discipline. Then there's the gap between licensing and airline eligibility. In the U.S., the 1,500-hour ATP rule (with reduced minimums for some degree programs) means years of instructing or other low-paid flying to build hours.

Finally, be realistic about how cyclical the hiring market is, and about early-career pay, seniority-based schedules, time away from home, recurring checkrides and the risk of losing your medical later. It's worth getting loss-of-license insurance, checking whether training providers are financially stable, and having a backup career plan.

Work backward from the flying job you want and the country where you intend to work. Check the licensing, medical, and work authorization requirements, and obtain the medical certificate your target career requires before making a large deposit. Map the steps from initial training through ratings, hour-building, and eligibility for your first paid flying job and, if that’s your goal, an airline seat.

Compare schools and routes on realistic total cost and time. Budget for extra flight hours, checkrides and retests, living expenses, loan interest, and time with little or no income. Ask schools how long recent students actually took, how often they could fly, and what graduates went on to do. Weather, aircraft and instructor availability, and examiner backlogs can stretch advertised timelines.

Finally, plan for the years after training. Find out which entry-level jobs are available where you can work, what they pay, and whether you’d need to relocate. Factor in hiring cycles, reserve schedules, commuting, and nights away, and leave yourself a financial fallback if training or hiring takes longer than expected.

Confirm early that you can obtain the medical certificate your goal requires. A commercial pilot licence lets you fly for pay, but your target airline may also require specific ratings, exams, or more flight experience.

For each training route, map out how you’ll get from your first lesson to your first paid flying job. Compare the full cost, including extra flight hours, exam fees, living expenses, loan interest, and time away from work. Ask schools how long recent students actually took and how weather, maintenance, and instructor availability affected their schedules.

Check how graduates built experience, what those jobs paid, and whether a cadet programme offers a job, an interview, or a chance to apply. Consider whether you can relocate, manage irregular schedules, and afford repayments if hiring slows or training takes longer than planned.
